question_en: A portfolio manager has compiled an investment's annual returns for three years: The average annual compounded return on the investment over the three-year holding period is closest to:
explanation_en:
The compounded periodic rate of return for an asset is the geometric mean return. It is used to measure the periodic average of investment
performance over multiple consecutive periods.
Compounding assumes that one period's ending investment value is the next period's beginning value (ie, that returns accumulate). The
geometric mean is the average periodic rate of return that accounts for compounding and includes accumulated returns in subsequent periods. In
this instance, there are three annual periods (ie, N = 3), so the geometric mean is:
(Choice B) 1.00% is the arithmetic mean, which is calculated as the simple average of multiple periodic returns and does not reflect
compounding.
(Choice C) 2.29% is the holding period return, which is the total cumulative return received over the three-year period, not the annual return.

question_en:
An investor deposits ¥100 million into a fund at the beginning of Year 1 and deposits another ¥50 million at the beginning of Year 2. At the beginning of Year 3, the investor withdraws ¥15 million. The fund has the following returns:

| Year 3 | Return (%) −20 |
|---|---|
| 1 | 20 |
| 2 | 10 |

The investor's money-weighted annual rate of return over the three-year period is closest to:
explanation_en:
The money-weighted return (MWR), an application of the internal rate of return (IRR), measures investment performance based on an
investor's cash flows (ie, deposits and withdrawals). By contrast, the arithmetic mean and time-weighted return do not account for cash flows into
and out of the portfolio.
As an application of the IRR, the MWR discounts cash flows so that their net present value (NPV) is equal to zero and the initial investment is
equal to the future discounted deposits and withdrawals. For the investor, deposits are outflows and withdrawals are inflows.
When calculating MWR, the investment's ending value is assumed to be the final cash inflow (if positive) or outflow (if negative). Therefore, to
calculate the MWR, the ending balance must be calculated first, using the investor's deposits and withdrawals and the return on the investment
over each period.
(¥ millions) Year 1 Year 2 Year 3
Balance at beginning of year 0 120 187
Investor's deposits (withdrawals) 100 50 −15
Net balance after deposits (withdrawals) 100 170 172
Return for the year 20% 10% −20%
Investment gain (loss) 20 17 −34.4
Balance at end of year [= Net balance + Investment gain (loss)] 120 187 137.6
After the cash flows have been identified, solve for the MWR using a financial calculator. Enter positive values for cash inflows and negative
values for cash outflows.

question_en: An individual makes the following deposits, one every six months with the first deposit beginning today: If the stated interest rate is 5.4% compounded monthly, the value of the account (in SGD) six months after the last deposit is made is closest to:
explanation_en:
This time value of money question requires the candidate to calculate the future value of a bank account that is funded by a series of three
unequal cash flows. The first deposit is made today, and subsequent deposits occur every six months.
Each deposit is a different amount, so the future value cannot be calculated as an annuity. Instead, each deposit's future value must be
calculated separately as the amount of the deposit (ie, its present value) multiplied by a future value factor:
The stated rate of 5.4% is compounded monthly, so there are 12 compounding periods per year. To account for monthly compounding, the stated
rate must be converted to a monthly rate: 0.054 ÷ 12 = 0.0045.
(Choice A) SGD 46,540 results from forgetting to compound for the 6-month period following the last deposit or from incorrectly assuming that all
deposits occur at the end of the period rather than at the beginning.
(Choice B) SGD 47,779 results from assuming semiannual, rather than monthly, compounding. It may be useful to remember that if two series
are identical with respect to the stated rate, amount, and timing of cash flows, the series with the more frequent compounding always produces a
higher future value.

question_en: A government issues a 20-year zero-coupon bond with a YTM of −0.02%. Five years later, economic conditions have improved, and the YTM is now 0.50%. Assuming annual compounding, the current price of the bond per 100 of par value is closest to:
explanation_en: Present value of a zero-coupon bond A bond's price is the PV of its expected returns, the coupon payments and par value, discounted by the market discount rate. A zero-coupon bond's price is simply the expected return of the par value, discounted by the market discount rate since there are no coupons. The investor typically purchases the zero-coupon bond at a discount to par and receives par at maturity. In this scenario, the bond was issued when the YTM was −0.02%, but since economic conditions have improved, the YTM increased to 0.50%. As the 20-year bond was issued five years ago, there are now 15 years until maturity. Using r = 0.50%, t = 15, and FV = 100, solve for the price of the bond as: = 100 / (1 + 0.005)15 = 92.7917 Alternatively, the solution can be obtained using a calculator: N = 15 FV = 100 I/Y = 0.5 PV = ─92.7917 ← solve It is important to understand the inverse relationship between the discount rate (r), the bond's yield, and PV (ie, the bond's price). The YTM increased from −0.02% to 0.50% after five years, and the bond's PV is now 92.7917. Had r remained at −0.02%, the PV would have been greater than that, at 100.3005 per 100 of par value (or 100 / 0.999815). However, the increase to r decreased the bond's PV. (Choice B) 97.5371 results from using a period of 5 years, instead of 15. (Choice C) 100.3005 results from discounting by the original YTM of −0.02%.

question_en: Three years ago, a government issued a 20-year zero coupon bond when the YTM was 4.5%. If this zero-coupon bond is now trading at 46.1778 per 100 of par value, then the market discount rate, assuming annual compounding, on this bond is closest to:
explanation_en: A bond's price is the PV of its expected returns, coupon payments, and par value, discounted by the market discount rate. A zero-coupon bond's price is simply the expected return of the par value, discounted by the market discount rate since there are no coupons. The investor typically purchases the zero-coupon bond at a discount to par and receives par at maturity. In this scenario, the bond has 17 years remaining to maturity, and the current price is 46.1778 per 100 of par value. Substitute 100 for the future (ie, par) value and 46.1778 for the PV to calculate the implied market discount rate (eg, YTM) of 0.0465 (or 4.65%). Alternatively, the solution can be obtained using a calculator: N = 17 FV = 100 PV = ─ 46.1778 I/Y = 4.65 ← Solve It is important to understand the inverse relationship between the yield (r) and price (PV). In this scenario, the YTM increased from 4.5% to 4.65% after three years and the PV is now 46.1778. Had r remained at 4.5%, the PV would have been greater, at 47.3176 per 100 of par value (or 100 / 1.04517). However, the increase in r decreases the bond's value. (Choice A) 3.94% results from incorrectly using the time since issuance, rather than the time to maturity. (Choice B) 4.60% results from assuming semiannual compounding.

explanation_en:
A dividend discount model (DDM) values a stock based on the PV of future dividends. A two-stage DDM contains:
an initial, finite period of high dividend growth (g ) for n years, followed by
S
a period of lower, sustainable growth (g ) into perpetuity.
L
The PV of the stock is the sum of the PV of the cash flows in each stage. The second stage can be valued as a perpetuity; the PV of that
perpetuity is the stock's terminal value. The stock's intrinsic value is the PV of the first stage's dividends plus the PV of the terminal value.
The terminal value represents the value of the stock at the end of the first stage: the PV of the second stage's discounted dividends at the end of
Year n. The discount rate is the required rate of return (r). In this scenario, the first stage is three years.

question_en: An annual coupon bond is currently trading at 98.50 per 100 of par value, with 9 years remaining to maturity. The current YTM is 9.00%. If the bond was issued exactly one year ago when the YTM was 8.90%, then the bond's price at issuance (per 100 of par) was closest to:
explanation_en:
A bond's price is calculated as the present value of its future cash flows: the periodic coupon payments and the par value at maturity. The
YTM is the implied market discount rate that equates the bond's discounted cash flows to its price. The YTM reflects the market's return
expectations given the bond's risk level.
In this scenario, at the end of Year 1 (t = 1), the bond is trading at 98.50, with 9 years left to maturity, based on a 9.00% YTM. The bond's annual
coupon payments of 8.75 can be derived from this information (PV = −98.5, n = 9, I/Y = 9, PMT = 8.75).
Given the coupon amount of 8.75, the price at the time of issuance can be derived from the coupon, the original maturity of the bond, and the
original YTM: (PMT = 8.75, I/Y = 8.9, n = 10, FV = 100, then PV = −99.0318).
The bond was originally issued at 99.03 per 100 of par when the YTM (ie, market discount rate) was 8.90%. One year later, the yield (ie, the
discount rate) has increased to 9.00%, the time to maturity has decreased (by one year) and the price (ie, PV) of the bond has decreased to 98.5
per 100 of par.
(Choice A) 98.40 results from incorrectly using 9.00%, which is the YTM at the end of Year 1, instead of the YTM at issuance.
(Choice C) 99.10 results from using the current time to maturity (9) instead of the maturity at issuance (10).

question_en: A distribution of returns has the same mean, standard deviation, and skewness as a normal distribution but has a kurtosis of 3.4. Compared with a normal distribution, this distribution indicates returns are more likely:
option_a: near the mean and in the extremes.
option_b: near the mean and less likely in the extremes.
option_c: in the extremes and less likely near the mean.
explanation_en: Skewness measures how nonsymmetrical a distribution is. Skewed distributions typically have more extreme values in one tail and more moderate values in the other. As a distribution becomes more skewed and either the left or right tail grows higher or longer, the values farther from the middle of the distribution are more likely to pull the arithmetic mean (simple mean or average) away from the distribution center than the median or mode. Because the arithmetic mean weights every value equally, it is more heavily influenced by outliers and extreme data points. A normal distribution, which is symmetrical, has a skewness of 0. A distribution with a skewness of 0.8 is positive, suggesting that there is a larger number of higher-valued data points. Since the tail to the right is longer in a distribution with positive skewness, the arithmetic mean is more affected than the median and mode. (Choice A) The mode (most common value) normally is least affected by skewness in a unimodal distribution. The presence of skewness in a distribution suggests a lack of symmetry (ie, one of the tails is higher or longer than the other). Altering the size of a distribution's tails typically will not change the most frequent data point. (Choice B) The median (middle value) is normally more affected than the mode by skewness in a unimodal distribution, although less affected than the arithmetic mean. In a positively skewed distribution, the greater number of larger values will pull the median to the right. Although the median is affected by the values in the right tail, the arithmetic mean is more affected by the larger values.

question_en: A positively skewed return distribution with a mean of 0% most likely has:
option_a: few extreme returns in the right tail.
option_b: frequent small returns in the right tail.
option_c: frequent extreme returns in the right tail.
explanation_en:
A normal distribution has returns that are symmetrically distributed around the mean. A skewed distribution, unlike a normal distribution, is
asymmetrical around the mean due to the greater presence of extreme outliers on one side. If the return distribution with a mean of 0% is:
positively skewed, it is characterized by frequent small losses (the left tail), and few extreme gains (the long right tail).
negatively skewed, it is characterized by frequent small gains (the right tail), and few extreme losses (the long left tail) (Choice B).
(Choice C) Skewed distributions will have few, not frequent, extreme results.

question_en:
A researcher collects the following sales data on 10 companies:

| Company A | B C | D E | F G H | I J |

| Sales ($ millions) 2.9 | 7.4 20 | 17.4 19.5 | 2.6 9.3 10.7 | 7.2 8.3 |

Based on this data, the second quintile for sales (in $ millions) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Deciles, quintiles, quartiles, and percentiles are all types of quantiles, which are measures of location for data sets. They provide the position
that a certain percentage of the data is at or below.
Quintiles split data sets into fifths. For instance, the 1st quintile marks the point at which 20% of the data is less than or equal, and the 2nd quintile
marks the point at which 40% of the data is less than or equal. To determine the value of the 2nd quintile, arrange the data in ascending order,
determine the location of the 2nd quintile, and match the associated value with that location.
Linear interpolation is one method to calculate the value for Location 4.4. The location of the 2nd quintile (4.4) equals the number of
observations plus one (10 + 1) multiplied by the 40 percent. The value of Location 4.4 is between the values of Locations 4 and 5. Since 4.4 is
40% of the distance between Locations 4 and 5, its value is 40% of the difference between 7.4 and 8.3:
(Choice A) 7.20 results from not adding 1 to the total number of observations in the location calculation.
(Choice C) 7.96 results from using 0.6, instead of 0.4, in the observation value calculation.

question_en: Which of the following most appropriately describes a property of the mode?
option_a: It can be used with nominal data.
option_b: It is the middle value of a distribution.

explanation_en: A skewed distribution is an asymmetrical probability distribution for which the mean is different than the median, which is different than the mode. The mean of a positively skewed distribution is greater than its median, which is greater than its mode (Choice A). Since the mean of a positively skewed distribution is greater than its median, more outcomes are negative than positive and the probability of a negative outcome is greater than the probability of a positive outcome. The number of expected negative outcomes is small and more likely whereas the number of expected positive outcomes is large but less likely. This distribution is depicted in the illustration on the right. (Choice B) A leptokurtic distribution (ie, "fat tails") is a symmetrical distribution that is more peaked than a normal distribution, and there are greater probabilities of extreme events in both tails. A skewed distribution has a greater probability of extreme events only in one tail.

question_en: An analyst collects P/E ratios from companies within an industry and plots them on a box and whisker chart: The third and fourth quartiles are closest to:
explanation_en: Mean absolute deviation (MAD) measures dispersion (ie, variability) of observations around the mean. Dispersion refers to the difference between an observation and the mean. Higher dispersion means that the observations are more spread out around the mean, which indicates a greater probability of observations that are significantly higher or lower than the mean. In finance, dispersion indicates risk. Since the sum of all dispersions around the mean equals 0, MAD instead uses the absolute value of each dispersion. The sum of all the absolute values is divided by the number of observations, which produces the average dispersion. The calculations are shown below: (Choice A) Data in a sample will be both above and below the mean, so some dispersions around the mean are negative and others are positive. The sum of all dispersions equals 0, so the average also equals 0. By using the absolute value of the dispersions, MAD always generates a number ≥ 0. (Choice C) 6.0 results from dividing the sum of the absolute values by (n − 1), or 4, instead of 5. The number of observations minus 1 is used only when calculating the standard deviation of a sample. MAD uses the actual number of observations.

question_en: An analyst determines that a return distribution has the same mean, standard deviation, and skewness as a normal distribution, but has an excess kurtosis of 2.2. If an analyst incorrectly assumes the returns are normally distributed, then in this analysis, extreme values would most likely be:
explanation_en: The harmonic mean is a weighted average. It is a measure of central tendency typically used for averaging ratios (stated as "amount per unit") where an observation's value is inversely proportional to its weight in the average. It can be used for cost averaging (ie, finding average price per share) when fixed amounts are invested periodically. In this instance, since the investor is investing annually the same total amount, €1,000,000, a lower stock price implies that a larger number of shares can be purchased. Thus, the lower (higher) share prices should be assigned larger (smaller) weights in the average since a greater (smaller) number of shares in the investment portfolio was purchased at that price. The harmonic mean assigns a larger weight to smaller observations and therefore is appropriate. (Choice B) The geometric mean is most appropriate for calculating the average growth rate over multiple consecutive return periods by taking compounding into account. It is not a weighted average. (Choice C) The arithmetic mean is a simple average of the purchase prices, assigning equal weight to all observations.

question_en:
An analyst compares the risk of Portfolio A to Portfolio B over the last four years and gathers the following information about both portfolios:

| Portfolio B Annual Returns (%) |
|---|
| -4 |
| 11 |
| 2 |
| -13 |

|  | Portfolio A | Portfolio B |
|---|---|---|
| Mean (%) | 1 | -1 |
| Range (%) | 23 |  |
| Mean Absolute Deviation | 8 |  |
| Sample Standard Deviation | 10.49 | 10.10 |

The comparison shows that Portfolio B is riskier in terms of the:
option_b: range and mean absolute deviation only.
option_c: range, mean absolute deviation, and standard deviation.
explanation_en:
To answer this question, you need to calculate only the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of Portfolio B. The range is included in each answer choice, and the standard deviations of both portfolios are given.

Mean absolute deviation (MAD), like standard deviation and range, is a measure of variability (dispersion) around a mean and can be used to gauge risk. MAD is calculated as follows:
1. Determine the mean of the observations.
2. Calculate the absolute difference between each observation and its mean (this eliminates the possibility of negative numbers).
3. Sum all the calculations from the previous step and divide the sum by the number of observations.

MAD for Portfolio B is calculated as:
Mean (Portfolio B) = (-4 + 11 + 2 - 13) / 4 = -1
MAD (Portfolio B) = (|-4 - (-1)| + |11 - (-1)| + |2 - (-1)| + |-13 - (-1)|) / 4 = (3 + 12 + 3 + 12) / 4 = 7.5

Portfolio B's range of returns [11 - (-13) = 24%] is greater than Portfolio A's range of returns (23%), so Portfolio B has greater risk in terms of range.

The MAD of Portfolio B (7.5) is less than the MAD of Portfolio A (8), which indicates that Portfolio B's returns have less variability around the mean and less risk than Portfolio A. The standard deviation of Portfolio B (10.10) is less than that of Portfolio A (10.49), also indicating less risk (Choices B and C).

Things to remember: Mean absolute deviation (MAD), like standard deviation and range, is a measure of variability (dispersion) around a mean and can be used to gauge risk. Less dispersion around the mean indicates less variability and less risk.

question_en: An analyst identifies the presence of outliers in a sample containing the P/E ratios of 40 companies. The analyst discards the two smallest and the two largest observations before calculating the average P/E ratio. This process best describes the use of a:
explanation_en:
Measures (ie, means) of central tendency include the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and weighted mean. Although the presence of extreme
values (ie, outliers) can significantly distort the accuracy of these measures, other measures reduce that effect. In this scenario, 40
observations are ranked in ascending order with three means applied that treat outliers in different ways:
A trimmed mean discards the smallest and largest observations and calculates the average of the remaining observations. In this case,
the 10% trimmed mean discards the two smallest observations (ranks 1 and 2) and the two largest observations (ranks 39 and 40), then
calculates the average of the remaining 36 observations.
A winsorized mean replaces the smallest and largest observations respectively with the smallest and largest values that fall within an
acceptable range. Here, the 90% winsorized mean replaces the two smallest values with 9.5 (rank 3) and the two largest values with 65.6
(rank 38), then calculates the average of the 40 observations (Choice C).
A harmonic mean is the ratio of the number of observations to the sum of reciprocals. It is a weighted average that assigns smaller
weights to larger observations; in this case, the weights range from 0.323 (rank 1) to 0.008 (rank 40). Due to these weights, the harmonic
mean is less influenced by large outliers, but it can be pulled significantly in the direction of smaller values (Choice B).

question_en: An analyst constructs the following histogram of S&P 500 Index annual returns: In this histogram, the median observation is in an interval that:
explanation_en:
A histogram's intervals are arranged in ascending order from left to right, each having the same interval width. Histograms are used to understand
a distribution's measures of central tendency. If a set of data contains an odd number of items, the median is the middle value. If the number of
items is even, the median is the number resulting from adding the two middle values together and dividing by 2.
In this scenario, there are 27 observations (ie, one per year from 1990 to 2016, inclusive), so the 14th observation is the median, which lies in
interval "10 ≤ x < 17":
The modal interval is the interval that contains the most observations. In this particular scenario, interval "10 ≤ x < 17", the interval that contains
the median, is also the modal interval (Choices B and C).
